title: Astronomers Spot First Milky Way Microquasar: Black Hole Powers Tiny Cosmic Jet
body:
Astronomers have identified the Milky Way’s first confirmed black‑hole‑driven microquasar, a compact system that launches powerful jets of matter at near‑light speed despite being cloaked by a dense veil of interstellar dust. The discovery, made using a combination of radio, infrared and X‑ray observations, provides a rare glimpse into how stellar‑mass black holes can mimic the behavior of their supermassive cousins and reshapes our understanding of high‑energy processes in our own galaxy.

The object, designated VLA J1855‑025, was first flagged as an unusual radio source in a survey of the Galactic plane conducted with the Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array. Subsequent infrared imaging with the Very Large Telescope revealed a faint, heavily reddened counterpart, while data from the Chandra X‑ray Observatory showed a persistent, hard X‑ray spectrum typical of accreting black holes. Most compelling, however, were the high‑resolution radio maps that displayed twin, oppositely directed jets extending several light‑years from the central engine—an unmistakable hallmark of a microquasar. Unlike previously known microquasars, which are powered by neutron stars or black holes that are relatively unobscured, VLA J1855‑025 lies behind a wall of dust that renders it virtually invisible in ordinary optical wavelengths.

Microquasars are scaled‑down versions of quasars, the luminous nuclei of distant galaxies powered by supermassive black holes. In both cases, matter spirals into the black hole, heating up and emitting intense radiation, while magnetic fields channel a fraction of the inflowing material into narrow, relativistic jets. The Milky Way has hosted a handful of confirmed microquasars, such as SS 433 and GRS 1915+105, but all have been linked to neutron‑star or black‑hole systems that are relatively easy to detect in visible light. The new find demonstrates that black‑hole‑driven microquasars can also lurk in the most opaque regions of the galaxy, hidden from conventional surveys.

The detection relied on a multi‑wavelength strategy that underscores the importance of coordinated observations across the electromagnetic spectrum. Radio telescopes can pierce through dust, revealing synchrotron emission from relativistic particles in the jets. Infrared instruments, less affected by extinction than optical cameras, can trace the heated dust and the donor star feeding the black hole. X‑ray observatories capture the high‑energy photons produced in the inner accretion disk. By stitching together these disparate data sets, researchers were able to confirm the presence of a compact object with a mass exceeding three solar masses—well within the black‑hole regime—and to map the geometry of its jets.

The existence of a black‑hole‑powered microquasar in such a dusty environment has several implications for astrophysics. First, it suggests that many more such systems may be concealed within the Galactic plane, awaiting discovery by radio and infrared surveys. Second, the jets from VLA J1855‑025 interact with the surrounding interstellar medium, compressing and heating gas clouds that could trigger or suppress star formation locally. Finally, studying the jet dynamics in a relatively nearby system offers a laboratory for testing theories of jet launching and collimation that are otherwise difficult to probe in distant quasars.

Looking ahead, astronomers plan to monitor VLA J1855‑025 with next‑generation facilities such as the Square Kilometre Array and the James Webb Space Telescope. Continuous radio imaging will track changes in jet morphology, while infrared spectroscopy could reveal the composition of the donor star and the accretion flow. As more hidden microquasars are uncovered, the census of black‑hole activity in the Milky Way will expand, refining models of how compact objects influence their galactic neighborhoods. The discovery of this dust‑shrouded microquasar marks a pivotal step toward a more complete picture of high‑energy phenomena in our own cosmic backyard.
